x: The emergency provisions are in Part XVIII, Articles 352–360. Part XX is amendment and Part XVI covers reservations for SCs, STs and others.
t: Recall Part XVIII and its Articles 352 to 360.

x: Article 352 covers war, external aggression or armed rebellion, 356 the failure of a State's constitutional machinery, and 360 a threat to India's financial stability. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i.
t: Recall the ground for each of the three emergencies.

x: Both are true: K.M. Nambiar called the emergency powers a 'fraud on the Constitution', and the Constitution provides three kinds of emergency. Their number does not explain his criticism, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether the number of emergencies explains a critic's view.

x: I and II are correct: a National Emergency needs a special majority in each House, and President's Rule a simple majority. III is false because a Financial Emergency needs only a simple majority.
t: Remember that only the National Emergency needs a special majority.

x: Option C is incorrect: since the 44th Amendment, a National Emergency must be approved within one month. President's Rule and a Financial Emergency have two months.
t: Discriminate one month (National) from two months (the other two).

x: A Financial Emergency under Article 360 has never been declared in India.
t: Recall which emergency has never been used.

x: Three are correct: National Emergencies were declared three times (1962, 1971, 1975), and President's Rule more than 100 times. Statement 3 is false because a Financial Emergency has never been declared.
t: Recall how often each emergency has been used.

x: In a National Emergency, Parliament can legislate on State subjects. Under President's Rule, the Assembly is dissolved or suspended and Parliament passes the State budget. In a Financial Emergency, financial directions can be given and pay cut. The answer is a-ii, b-iii, c-i.
t: Match each emergency to its main effect.

x: Both are true: Article 358 applies only to emergencies for war or external aggression, and it suspends Article 19 automatically. That it is automatic does not explain why its grounds are limited, so R does not explain A.
t: Ask whether automatic operation explains limited grounds.

x: A is true: Article 359 suspends the right to go to court to enforce specified fundamental rights. B is false because Article 359 applies in external emergencies and in armed rebellion.
t: Discriminate Article 358 (external only) from 359 (armed rebellion too).

x: Under Article 354, the President can change the division of revenues between the Centre and States during a National Emergency, until the end of that financial year.
t: Recall Article 354.

x: I and III are correct: Parliament can extend the Houses' terms one year at a time, and its laws on State subjects lapse six months after the Emergency ends. II is false because no extension can run beyond six months after the Emergency.
t: Recall the six-month limit after an Emergency ends.

x: Article 358 suspends Article 19 automatically, Article 359 needs a separate Presidential order, and Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended. The answer is a-iii, b-ii, c-i.
t: Discriminate automatic suspension (358) from suspension by order (359).

x: Both are true: President's Rule can go beyond a year only if a National Emergency is in force and the Election Commission certifies that elections cannot be held, up to three years in all. R explains A.
t: Recall the two conditions for extending President's Rule.

x: Emergencies were declared in 1962 and 1971, then on 25 June 1975, and the last was lifted on 21 March 1977. The order is B, D, A, C.
t: Recall the years 1962, 1971, 1975 and 1977.

x: The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion' as a ground under Article 352. Option C reverses this.
t: Recall the 44th Amendment's change of wording.

x: All four are correct: the 44th Amendment cut approval to one month, protected Articles 20 and 21, required the Cabinet's written advice, and replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'.
t: Recall the 44th Amendment's safeguards.

x: Three are correct: a National Emergency needs a special majority, and President's Rule and a Financial Emergency need simple majorities. Statement 4 is false because a National Emergency has no maximum period.
t: Discriminate the three-year cap (President's Rule) from no cap (National Emergency).

x: Both are true: under Article 356, the President can impose President's Rule on the Governor's report or otherwise, when a State cannot be governed according to the Constitution.
t: Recall Article 356's ground.

x: A National Emergency continues six months at a time with no limit, President's Rule six months at a time up to three years, and a Financial Emergency until revoked. The answer is a-i, b-ii, c-iii.
t: Recall how long each emergency can last.

x: All three are correct: if the Lok Sabha is dissolved, any of the three proclamations survives until 30 days after the new Lok Sabha first sits, by which time it must be approved.
t: Recall the 30-day rule after dissolution.

x: The 1975 Emergency was declared on 25 June 1975 on the ground of 'internal disturbance' and lifted on 21 March 1977.
t: Recall 25 June 1975.

x: Two are correct: Article 358 suspends Article 19 automatically, and Article 359 needs a separate order. Statements 3 and 4 are false: Articles 20 and 21 can never be suspended, and Article 358 does not apply to armed rebellion.
t: Discriminate Article 358 (external only) from 359 (armed rebellion too).

x: Option C is incorrect: Parliament's laws on State subjects made during an Emergency lapse six months after it ends. They do not last for ever.
t: Recall the six-month lapse rule.

x: Both are true: under Article 354, the President can change the revenue division during an Emergency, and the change lasts until the end of the financial year in which the Emergency ends.
t: Recall Article 354.

x: A National Emergency needs the Cabinet's written advice, Parliament's State-subject laws lapse six months after it ends, revenue changes last to the end of the financial year, and 1975's was declared on 25 June. The answer is a-iii, b-iv, c-i, d-ii.
t: Recall each emergency rule's time limit.

x: Option D is incorrect: a Financial Emergency has no maximum period and lasts until the President revokes it. During it, salaries, including judges', can be cut and financial directions given.
t: Discriminate the three-year cap (President's Rule) from no cap (Financial Emergency).

x: Both are true: only a National Emergency touches fundamental rights, through Articles 358 and 359. President's Rule and a Financial Emergency do not suspend them directly.
t: Recall which emergency affects fundamental rights.
